description: We are a team of IT students passionate about technology, innovation, and problem-solving. We aim to build an innovative solution to a real-world problem that can benefit our community. We are looking for motivated participants with skills in programming, AI, data analysis, UI/UX, or other useful fields. If you enjoy challenges, teamwork, and creating meaningful solutions, we would be happy to have you join us
summary: Our team designed and built Project SuperMoon to bring daily crew-health information into one place. Crew members record 15 measurements covering sleep, heart activity, reaction time, wellbeing and workload. After seven consecutive daily calibration records, eligible records can receive a next-day fatigue forecast when the model service is available, with explanations and trends to help interpret it. Five fictional alert examples show why a concern happening now should be considered separately from tomorrow's forecast. NASA human research resources informed the design. We tested the connected application using synthetic data; evaluation with suitable human measurements is a next step.
details:
Our team designed and developed Project SuperMoon for the challenge of creating health-monitoring software for astronauts. We wanted to make daily observations easier to understand together: a change in sleep may matter more when it appears alongside heavier workload, slower reactions or a change in wellbeing. Our goal is to help a crew member follow those patterns and prepare a clearer record for discussion with medical support.

We built a dashboard that collects 15 measurements and an optional journal entry. The first seven consecutive daily records establish a personal baseline. From the eighth record, eligible new observations can receive a forecast when the model service is available. A trained Random Forest uses 26 current, baseline and recent-history features to produce a next-day fatigue category and a prototype fatigue index. Three SHAP explanations identify the inputs that contributed most to that result. Users can review earlier records, compare measurements with their baseline and read a source-linked guide. The explanations describe the model's calculation; they do not identify medical causes.

An important design decision was to separate current concerns from tomorrow's forecast. The interface includes five fictional alert examples, including a serious current concern alongside a low example forecast for the next day. This shows why a reassuring forecast should not erase a concern that needs attention now. These examples are predefined presentation content. The complete Clinical Alert V2 engine is deferred, so these five examples do not execute its 14 acceptance cases.

The app also includes a custom 60-response reaction-time task with random waits. A shorter ten-response practice mode cannot transfer its results into the model's 60-response fields. Attention-task accuracy must be measured externally and entered manually. The reaction task is inspired by psychomotor-vigilance research; it has not been validated as a standard PVT or NASA assessment.

We implemented the interface with Angular, Ionic and TypeScript, connected it to a TypeScript backend and a local Python model service, and provided Windows packaging and a Linux launch path. The same interface runs in a browser. After installation, ordinary model inference runs locally without an external AI API. The repository and application retain their development name, ASTRA-SHIELD / Crew Health Console.

We used a seeded Python simulation to create 7,200 forecast records from 120 simulated participants, with separate training, validation and test participants. No measured NASA astronaut records were imported. The selected fatigue classifier achieved validation Macro-F1 of 0.5273 and historical test Macro-F1 of 0.5285. These are simulation results, not clinical accuracy measurements. NASA's human-spaceflight hazards and risks resources informed the Guide; Standard Measures and ARCHER informed the idea of consistent personal observations; Reaction Self Test background motivated the reaction-time demonstration. These references did not supply our numerical data or validate the model.

We tested the connected interface, backend and model through calibration, prediction, explanations, invalid inputs, saved-record retries and mobile layouts. The latest source passed 81 UI checks, 48 end-to-end integration checks and 28 focused regression checks, with additional frontend and production-dashboard tests. The updated Windows package also passed native tests of both its portable and installed executable. These checks establish software behavior; evaluation with suitable human measurements remains a next step.

Our team defined the idea, requirements, interface direction and development decisions. Each member contributed to building and reviewing the project.

Yazan Ehmaid, a third-year medical student, reviewed the selected measurements, their definitions and their interpretation, and provided medical input on the measurement workflow and proposed alerts. His contribution helped us assess the scientific rationale behind our choices. This was a medical and scientific review within the team, rather than clinical validation of the model.

Taleen Abualhasan independently developed the original backend. As a developer with experience in machine learning and model training, she also contributed to training, evaluating and reviewing the models. Karam Alhams developed the original frontend and translated the team’s requirements into the dashboard and user experience.

Majdi Abu Ahour coordinated the selection and organization of the data and supporting resources, focusing on why each measurement mattered to the project. Together with Yazan and Taleen, he reviewed data quality, cleaning requirements, internal consistency and the scientific basis for the selected measurements. The numerical training records remained synthetic throughout this process. Majdi also connected the frontend, backend and model service into the integrated application.

Omar Hemadneh tested the project, checked edge cases and reviewed security concerns. His work helped identify unexpected behavior and areas needing further attention before the demonstration. Mahfuoz Asa'ad Kamal Izhiman managed the team, coordinated responsibilities and reviewed progress and completed work. He also worked with Majdi on preparing the presentation.

SI tools helped accelerate implementation and verification throughout this team-led process. OpenAI ChatGPT/Codex assisted with simulation code and journal templates, model analysis, integration, debugging, automated tests, Windows packaging, documentation and presentation editing. Karam’s original frontend acknowledges Claude, by Anthropic, assistance with code, Guide text and SVG illustrations, including the astronaut and watch. The repository records these contributions and data origins in its documentation and machine-readable PROVENANCE.json metadata. The application and revised presentation visibly identify the SI-generated artwork.

Our next steps are to evaluate the workflow with its intended users, study how real measurements compare with the simulator, and implement and validate the complete alert engine. The current prototype is a research and demonstration tool, not a medical diagnosis or clearance to perform a critical task.
